source.title: A Mean Field Theory of Batch Normalization
source.authors: Greg Yang; Jeffrey Pennington; Vinay Rao; Jascha Narain Sohl-Dickstein; S. Schoenholz

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how batch-normalized network depth affects trainability using empirical simulations, a different setup from the version’s plain convolutional networks and training-error measure.
record.gate_note: The depth experiments report test accuracy and whether networks are trainable, not training classification error. The CIFAR100 training-accuracy sweep in Fig. 8 is figure-only and its individual settings and values cannot be reliably reconstructed from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study bears on V4 through experiments varying initial batch-normalization scales and offsets to improve trainable depth, and explicitly reported training acceleration from positive offset initialization. R1–R2 do not test V3's training-error comparison in convolutional networks.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors derive initialization-time gradient explosion under stated mean-field assumptions, connect it to depth limits, and show that approaching a linear activation regime reduces explosion and improves trainability. They also report rapid gradient equilibration after an optimization step and improvements from tuning epsilon.
record.recipe_differences: Empirical fully connected batch-normalized networks with rectified-linear activations; depth and batch-size sweeps, with test accuracy as the plotted outcome. The versions describe several other architectures, interventions and measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Depth; batch size; optimizer; activation linearity parameters (γ or β); ε.

fits_no_version.finding: Fully connected batch-normalized ReLU networks have a reported trainability boundary near 50 layers, assessed using test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the tested initialization and training recipes, increasing depth beyond roughly 50 layers prevents successful learning in fully connected batch-normalized ReLU networks.

fits_no_version.finding: At initialization, gradients explode with depth under the theory's fixed-point and gradient-independence assumptions; changing weight variances cannot eliminate this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stacked batch normalization can cause initialization-time gradient explosion in wide fully connected networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing the batch-normalization epsilon parameter improves trainable depth and can accelerate VGG19 training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The batch-normalization epsilon setting affects optimization even when normalization remains present.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient magnitudes rapidly equilibrate after an optimization step, while relative gradient vanishing can leave early layers nearly unchanged in deeper networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initial gradient explosion in batch-normalized networks can produce subsequent relative gradient vanishing.

record.problems: The central depth results are plotted as test accuracy, not training classification error. The text gives an approximate depth boundary for MNIST but not CIFAR10; the plots do not provide numerical uncertainty for these training-depth results.
record.rows_left_out: The CIFAR100 VGG19 training-accuracy and validation-accuracy sweeps in Figs. 8–9 are figure-only and cover many learning-rate, β-initialization, ε and epoch combinations; individual values and condition mappings cannot be reliably recovered from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error in sufficiently large CNNs, including random or corrupted labels. The declared VGG19 accuracy sweeps do not establish this endpoint.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious local minima, and student overparameterization.
Training-error degradation with depth in plain batch-normalized CNNs, longer-training controls, identity-shortcut comparisons, special plain-tanh initializations, and Fixup.
Activation-matched weight-initialization comparisons in unnormalized networks, Gaussian versus orthogonal weights, and orthogonal convolution kernels at extreme depths.
Learning rates relative to an initial stability threshold, curvature reduction during recovery, and edge-of-stability dynamics.
Training speed and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, and comparisons with Fixup.

missing.what: Qualitative initialization-versus-trainable-depth results: decreasing initial gamma in tanh networks and increasing initial beta in ReLU networks significantly increase maximum trainable depth. Record these separately, identifying test accuracy as the operational measure and leaving numerical boundaries unreadable.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. Remove the record's V3 limits_scope verdict: architectural differences and an unmeasured training-error outcome are untested parts, not evidence limiting V3. V4 support is qualitative and rests on the supplied text; individual VGG19 sweep values were already declared left out.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report whether sufficiently large convolutional networks reach zero or near-zero training classification error, including with corrupted or random labels.
No teacher-student ReLU experiments or neuron-width comparisons.

Tests fully connected batch-normalized networks on MNIST and CIFAR10 using test accuracy to assess trainability by depth, not training error in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks versus residual networks. Does not test ImageNet or the stated special initializations or Fixup.
No comparison of Gaussian and orthogonal initialization or test of activation-matched initialization for training speed or trainable depth.
No learning-rate stability-limit or sharpness experiments.
No direct comparison of batch normalization with no normalization for training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and no Fixup comparison.

rows.subject: rectified linear networks with batch normalization
rows.operation_detail: Varied network depth and batch size; plotted test accuracy after training.
rows.measure: Test accuracy; authors describe networks deeper than about 50 layers as untrainable regardless of batch size.
rows.note: The text states the approximate depth boundary, but the version predicts training error; test accuracy does not directly measure that outcome.
rows.check: The subject is a fully connected network. Test accuracy after 10 epochs and the authors' stated depth boundary do not establish V3's higher training classification error in plain convolutional networks or the benefit of identity shortcuts.

rows.subject: rectified linear networks with batch normalization
rows.operation_detail: Varied network depth and batch size; plotted test accuracy after training.
rows.measure: Test accuracy; the text says the trainable region is nearly identical to the other batch-size and optimizer experiments.
rows.note: No numerical depth boundary or training-error result is stated specifically for CIFAR10.
rows.check: The subject is a fully connected network. Test accuracy after 50 epochs does not measure V3's training-error effect, and no residual-network comparison is reported. The text also describes nearly identical trainable regions across all Fig. 3 experiments.

relationships.condition: Fully connected batch-normalized tanh and ReLU networks on MNIST; initial activation scale or offset varied
relationships.reason: Section 4 and Fig. 5(a,b) explicitly report greater maximum trainable depth as initial gamma decreases or beta increases toward a linear activation regime; this qualitative result is missing from the rows.
relationships.display_finding: Decreasing initial gamma or increasing beta toward a linear activation regime increased maximum trainable depth.
